title: Avicenna’s Flying Man — can you know yourself without sensing your body?
when: Developed by the Persian philosopher and physician Avicenna (Ibn Sīnā, c. 980–1037), especially in the eleventh-century Psychology of The Healing; exact dating of individual formulations is uncertain.
people: Avicenna; later interpreters include medieval Islamic philosophers and contemporary scholars of consciousness.
origin: The Arabic-language philosophical tradition of the medieval Islamic world, drawing on and critically extending Greek philosophy, especially Aristotelian psychology.
idea: Imagine a fully formed person suddenly created, suspended in empty space, with limbs apart and every sense deprived of input. Avicenna says this person would still affirm that he exists, despite having no awareness of his body. The thought experiment directs attention to a basic first-person awareness that, Avicenna argues, is not simply assembled from sensory perceptions. He uses it to suggest that the soul is distinct from the body, but what exactly the scenario establishes remains contested: scholars disagree about whether its central point is self-awareness, the soul’s essence, or the soul’s separability. It does not show that ordinary human life is actually disembodied, or settle every question about mind and body.
relevance: The Flying Man gives an unusually vivid test case for current debates about consciousness: is there a minimal sense of “I” beneath perception, memory, and bodily awareness? Contemporary discussions of minimal selfhood, embodiment, and sensory deprivation revisit its question while also challenging the idea that self-awareness can be isolated from bodily and social processes. Its enduring value may be less a final proof than a way to make competing intuitions about experience visible.
